mcqs.question: Which position value removes an element from normal flow but keeps it anchored to the viewport regardless of page scroll?
options: sticky
fixed
relative
static
mcqs.explanation: fixed removes the element from flow and anchors it to the viewport (or a transformed ancestor), so it stays put no matter how far the page scrolls. sticky is scroll-dependent — relative and static both stay in normal flow.

mcqs.question: A card component sets `position: relative` with no top/left/right/bottom offsets. What does this declaration actually do?
options: Nothing, since relative requires an offset to have any effect
It nudges the card slightly based on its default margin
It creates a positioning anchor so any absolutely positioned child anchors to the card instead of a further-up ancestor
It removes the card from normal flow so siblings ignore its space
mcqs.explanation: relative with no offset produces no visible nudge, but it still creates a positioning context for descendants — an absolute child will now anchor to this element's box instead of drifting to the next positioned ancestor up the tree. relative never removes an element from flow; that's absolute and fixed.

mcqs.question: Element A has `z-index: 9999` but sits inside a parent with `opacity: 0.99`. Element B, a sibling of the parent, has `z-index: 2` and no special properties. Which renders on top?
options: A, because 9999 is a higher explicit value than 2
Whichever comes later in the source order, since the z-index values are being compared incorrectly
B, because the parent's opacity created a new stacking context, so A's z-index only competes against its own siblings inside that context
Neither — opacity below 1 makes an element render below all positioned elements
mcqs.explanation: opacity < 1 creates a stacking context around the parent, so A's z-index of 9999 is only meaningful when compared to its siblings inside that same context. Against B, it's the parent's position in the outer stacking order that counts, and the parent has no elevated z-index — so B wins.

mcqs.question: A dropdown with `z-index: 9999` still renders behind a sticky header with `z-index: 100`. The dropdown's parent card has `transform: translateY(0)` for an animation. What's the most direct fix?
options: Increase the dropdown's z-index even further, since 9999 clearly isn't being applied
Remove the header's `position: sticky` so it no longer competes for stacking
Set the dropdown's position to `static` so it stops trying to stack
Remove the unwanted `transform` from the card (or render the dropdown outside that subtree, e.g. via a portal)
mcqs.explanation: The card's transform creates a stacking context that traps the dropdown's z-index inside it — the dropdown only outranks siblings within the card, not the header outside it. Raising the dropdown's own z-index further changes nothing, since the comparison never crosses the context boundary; removing the transform or moving the dropdown out of that subtree does.

mcqs.question: You need a table-of-contents heading that scrolls normally at first, then pins to the top of the viewport once the user scrolls past it. Which position value fits?
options: fixed
sticky
absolute
relative
mcqs.explanation: sticky is exactly the hybrid case: it behaves like relative (scrolls normally) until a scroll threshold, then behaves like fixed within its containing block. fixed would pin the element from page load instead of only after scrolling past it.
